clue.text: Original form of floodlighting?

parts.note: the first lighting in the Flood would be Noah's Ark lamp, which sounds like an electric lamp that throws a bright arc of light

explanation.surface: A question about how stadium floodlights were first made.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Floodlighting' is read as lighting during Noah's Flood: an ark lamp, which is said the same as the carbon-arc lamp used in early floodlights.
explanation.definitionFit: Early floodlights used carbon electrodes that made a brilliant electric arc, the earliest powerful lamp of its kind.

clue.text: This book tells us what its characters are for

definitions.text: This book tells us what its characters are for

parts.words: This book tells us what its characters are for
parts.note: a child's primer says 'A is for apple, B is for ball', telling what each letter stands for

explanation.surface: A novel that explains the purpose of each person in its story.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Characters' suggests people in a story, but here it means letters, as in an 'A is for apple' children's book.
explanation.definitionFit: A children's letter book runs through every letter in order, saying what each one is for.

clue.text: Dobbin gets his priorities wrong !

parts.note: putting the cart before the horse is the idiom for getting things in the wrong order; Dobbin is a stock name for a farm horse

explanation.surface: An old farm horse confuses what matters most.
explanation.walkthrough: Dobbin is a traditional English name for a plodding farm horse; the idiom 'put the cart before the horse' means doing things in the wrong order, and the answer literally puts CART before HORSE.
explanation.definitionFit: A draught animal that pulls a farm wagon is the kind of horse Dobbin is.

clue.text: The tone of a French father is grave

definitions.text: The tone of a French father is grave

parts.words: The tone of a French father is grave
parts.note: the French word for father, père, carries a grave mark over its e, and tone also means the stress or lilt of speech

explanation.surface: A remark that a Frenchman's dad speaks solemnly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grave' reads as solemn, but it is the grave mark over the e in père; 'tone' is the other sense, a manner of speaking.
explanation.definitionFit: Both a written mark over a letter and a regional way of speaking share this word.

clue.text: What a face to make when put out about nothing!

definitions.text: What a face to make when put out about nothing!

indicators.note: about means the word put goes round the O for nothing

parts.note: taken as written, the word put
nothing is zero, the letter O

explanation.surface: A sulky expression is the face you pull when annoyed over nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put out' doubles as annoyed; mechanically 'about' wraps PUT round O, nothing, and 'out' links.
explanation.definitionFit: Pushing the lips forward in sulky displeasure is the face someone annoyed makes.

clue.text: A Regency poem ? No, one on husbandry

definitions.text: A Regency poem ? No, one on husbandry

parts.words: A Regency poem ? No, one on husbandry
parts.note: the name sounds like a poem of the era of the Georges, the Regency, but it is a poem about farming, after Virgil's

explanation.surface: Someone guesses a poem is from the Regency era and is corrected.
explanation.walkthrough: The Regency fell in the Georgian period, so a poem named after George seems to belong there; in fact the word, from Virgil's Georgics, means a poem on farming.
explanation.definitionFit: Virgil's verses on tilling and livestock gave their name to any poem on agriculture.

clue.text: Keats's sylvan historian

parts.note: in his famous ode Keats addresses an ancient vase painted with woodland scenes as a 'Sylvan historian'

explanation.surface: A woodland chronicler described by the poet Keats.
explanation.walkthrough: Keats's ode opens by calling the vase 'Sylvan historian', since its painted figures tell a rustic tale.
explanation.definitionFit: The decorated ancient Greek vessel in Keats's ode tells a woodland story in pictures.

clue.text: Can't go so wildly with figures of eight!

indicators.note: wildly says the letters of the preceding words are thrown into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone told not to move wildly when skating figure-of-eight shapes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wildly' rearranges CANTGOSO. 'Figures of eight' is not the skating loop: it means shapes with eight sides.
explanation.definitionFit: A polygon with eight sides is a figure of eight sides.

clue.text: Lunar composition, no longer acceptable?

parts.note: folklore said the moon was made of unripe ..., an idea nobody now accepts

explanation.surface: A theory of what the moon is made of that is now out of favour.
explanation.walkthrough: The old saying held that the moon is made of unripe (green) cheese; the question mark admits the idea is no longer believed.
explanation.definitionFit: Folk tales held that the moon was made of new, unripened curd.

clue.text: See 7
A drop in the ocean? This could help

definitions.text: A drop in the ocean? This could help

parts.words: A drop in the ocean? This could help
parts.note: a drop here is a fall from a plane into the sea, which a canopy slows

explanation.surface: A tiny contribution that might still be of some use.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A drop in the ocean' is the idiom for a tiny amount, but read literally it is a fall from an aircraft into the sea.
explanation.definitionFit: A canopy that slows a person falling from an aircraft helps any descent, seaward or not.

clue.text: Sheet-changing for more than one here

indicators.note: changing says the letters of sheet are altered into another order

explanation.surface: Changing the bed linen in a room for several guests.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Changing' rearranges SHEET. The definition is a pointer word: 'this' for one item here, its plural for several.
explanation.definitionFit: The demonstrative for nearby items in the plural points at several things close by.

clue.text: Capital at getting the birds

parts.note: hens are birds

explanation.surface: Someone in a city being jeered or getting the bird.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Getting the bird' is a theatre phrase for being hissed, but here AT simply takes HENS.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek seat of government is a capital city.

clue.text: The cynical old tub-thumper ?

parts.note: the Greek Cynic philosopher famously lived in a large tub or jar, so he is a tub-thumper in a literal sense

explanation.surface: A jaded old ranting public speaker.
explanation.walkthrough: A tub-thumper is a ranting orator; the Greek philosopher of the Cynic school lived in a tub, and the C of 'cynical' points to his school.
explanation.definitionFit: The ancient founder figure of the Cynic school of philosophy reputedly slept in a tub.

clue.text: Time of Times

parts.note: the time is half past four, and four times thirty is a multiplication, so the times-table reading gives the clock reading

explanation.surface: A question about when the Times newspaper comes out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Times' suggests the newspaper, but read as multiplication the numbers four and thirty, said together, are a clock time.
explanation.definitionFit: Half past four in the afternoon is written as the hour followed by thirty minutes.

clue.text: Organs in rehearsal

indicators.note: in says the word sits inside the letters of rehearsal

explanation.surface: Church organs being played in a practice session.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Organs' suggests church instruments, but means body parts.
explanation.definitionFit: Body parts for hearing are sense organs.

clue.text: How can those living there feel on top of the world ?

definitions.text: How can those living there feel on top of the world

parts.words: How can those living there feel on top of the world
parts.note: Australians live at the bottom of the globe yet the idiom 'on top of the world' means elated, a paradox

explanation.surface: A puzzled question about how happy some people can be.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On top of the world' means delighted; the joke is that the people meant live at the bottom of the globe, in Australia and New Zealand.
explanation.definitionFit: The nickname for Australia and New Zealand refers to their place on the far side of the globe.

clue.text: Extension on pitch for the players

definitions.text: Extension on pitch for the players

parts.words: Extension on pitch for the players
parts.note: a pitch is a football field, and the referee may add further minutes for the teams to play on

explanation.surface: A musical performance lengthened for the band.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pitch' and 'players' suggest music, but the pitch is a football field and the players a team.
explanation.definitionFit: Additional minutes added to a drawn football match lengthen the playing period.

clue.text: It caused the downfall of a miner's daughter

definitions.text: It caused the downfall of a miner's daughter

parts.words: It caused the downfall of a miner's daughter
parts.note: in the song 'Clementine', the miner's daughter hit her foot on a sliver of wood and fell into the water

explanation.surface: Something brought about the ruin of a mining family's girl.
explanation.walkthrough: In the American folk song 'Oh My Darling, Clementine', the miner's daughter stubs her toe against a sliver of wood and falls into the foaming brine.
explanation.definitionFit: A sharp sliver of wood tripped the girl in the song, making her fall.

clue.text: Drinks deeply and awakens many for a start

indicators.note: for a start says the letter for many comes at the front

parts.note: C is the Roman numeral for a hundred, taken as many
awakens means arouses

explanation.surface: Someone drinks a lot and wakes up lots of people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Many' gives C, a hundred in Roman numerals; 'for a start' puts it ahead of AROUSES.
explanation.definitionFit: To revel and drink freely is to booze heavily.

clue.text: She'll do work if you twist her arm, or type

indicators.note: twist says the letters of arm, or and type are wrung into a new order

explanation.surface: A secretary who will only type if you twist her arm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Twist her arm' looks like the idiom for persuading, but 'twist' rearranges ARMORTYPE. The answer is the noun, a temp: an office worker hired for a short spell.
explanation.definitionFit: A stand-in office worker hired short-term is a temp, the noun from the adjective.

clue.text: Direction to a porch

parts.note: S, south, is a compass direction

explanation.surface: Instructions on how to reach a porch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Direction' is S, south.
explanation.definitionFit: A covered colonnade in ancient Greece was a roofed walkway, a porch.

clue.text: All at sea with a petty cash allowance

explanation.surface: Confused over the small office expense fund.
explanation.walkthrough: 'All at sea' reads as confused, but here it means literally on the water; a float is a sum of loose change kept for small expenses.
explanation.definitionFit: Floating on the water is one sense; the other is one sum of small change kept for minor expenses.

clue.text: Played to Jack on the green

definitions.text: Played to Jack on the green

parts.words: Played to Jack on the green
parts.note: in lawn bowls the small target ball is the jack, and players send their woods towards it on the green

explanation.surface: Someone performed for a man named Jack on the village green.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jack' looks like a man's name, but in lawn bowls (a British green-sward game) it is the small target ball.
explanation.definitionFit: Rolling a wood towards the target in lawn bowls is the past-tense action of this game.

clue.text: Flight round a pole, or over a door

indicators.note: round says the word flight goes about the other letters

parts.note: N, north, is one of the poles

explanation.surface: A flight path circling a pole, or perhaps over a door.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Round' puts FLIGHT round A and N (north pole). The definition names where the thing is: a window over a door.
explanation.definitionFit: A half-moon window set above a doorway sits over the door.

clue.text: She has three points, thank you

parts.note: N, E and S are three points of the compass
ta is British slang for thank you

explanation.surface: A woman with three good qualities says thanks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Three points' are compass points N, E, S; 'ta' is everyday British for thanks.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman's given name, so it stands for a female person.

clue.text: To get a duck in an island

parts.note: to bag is to get or catch
a duck is a score of nought in cricket, the letter O

explanation.surface: Going duck hunting on an island.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A duck' is a zero score in cricket, giving O; 'get' gives BAG.
explanation.definitionFit: The Caribbean partner island of Trinidad is an island.

clue.text: He sounds an unsuitable employer of an old soldier

definitions.text: He sounds an unsuitable employer of an old soldier

parts.words: He sounds an unsuitable employer of an old soldier
parts.note: the saying runs 'old soldiers never die', so someone whose job title says 'die-er' would find an old soldier useless

explanation.surface: A man who seems the wrong boss for a veteran.
explanation.walkthrough: The proverb 'Old soldiers never die'; the cloth-colouring trade's name is said like 'die-er', one who dies, a job no old soldier could do.
explanation.definitionFit: A tradesman who colours cloth is a man, matching the clue's 'He'.

clue.text: Shoot here, in the attack

explanation.surface: An order to open fire at this spot in an assault.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shoot' reads as fire, but means filming: a film is shot on the stage set; the other sense is the beginning of an assault.
explanation.definitionFit: Filming takes place on the stage set; also, the start of an assault is the first attack.

clue.text: Knotty problems at the Palace ?

parts.note: knotty refers to neckties, which at the Palace are worn by the monarch's family, and the answer read as two words says so

explanation.surface: Difficult issues facing the royal household.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Knotty problems' suggests tricky matters, but split as royal ties it means the knotted neckwear of the royal family; whole, it means an author's earnings.
explanation.definitionFit: Payments to an author per copy sold come from the word for crowned persons, split it becomes ties.

clue.text: A twinkling bat resembled this cupbearer

definitions.text: A twinkling bat resembled this cupbearer

parts.words: A twinkling bat resembled this cupbearer
parts.note: in Alice in Wonderland the Hatter sings 'Twinkle, twinkle, little bat ... like a tray for tea in the sky'

explanation.surface: A glittering bat looked like a waiter carrying cups.
explanation.walkthrough: The Mad Hatter's parody in Alice in Wonderland: 'Up above the world you fly, like a [tray for tea] in the sky'; 'cupbearer' is something that carries cups.
explanation.definitionFit: A flat board for carrying cups and saucers bears the cups.

clue.text: Don again set right

explanation.surface: Putting clothes back on to put matters straight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Don' reads as a name or a tutor, but means put on clothes; to clothe again is to re-dress.
explanation.definitionFit: Clothing a person once more is one sense; making amends for a wrong is the other.
